paragraphs.heading: Clocks run slower near mass
paragraphs.text: Gravitational time dilation is a real difference in how much time passes for observers at different distances from a mass. The closer a clock sits to the source of gravity, where the gravitational potential is lower, the slower its time passes. Move the clock away and it speeds up. So clocks near massive bodies run more slowly than clocks far from them.

paragraphs.heading: Where the idea comes from
paragraphs.text: Einstein first described the effect in 1907, as a result of special relativity applied to frames of reference that are accelerating. The bridge to gravity is the equivalence principle: in general relativity, any accelerated frame is physically the same as a gravitational field of equal strength. In the full theory, the effect is a difference in how proper time passes from one position to another, as described by the metric tensor of spacetime. Tests of the theory have since confirmed it.

paragraphs.heading: How big is it on Earth
paragraphs.text: On Earth the effect is tiny. Atomic clocks at different heights eventually show different times, but the gaps are measured in nanoseconds. Over Earth's whole 4.6 billion years, though, a clock at about 9,000 meters would be about 39 hours ahead of one at sea level, and the planet's core is effectively 2.5 years younger than its surface. Leaving out rotation, a clock on Earth's surface builds up about 0.0219 fewer seconds a year than a distant clock, while one on the Sun's surface builds up about 66.4 fewer seconds.

paragraphs.heading: Light feels it too
paragraphs.text: Gravitational time dilation is closely tied to gravitational redshift. When something gives off light of a constant frequency close to a massive body, its time is slowed, so an observer far away measures that light at a lower, redshifted frequency. Locally, nothing looks odd: anyone measuring the speed of light where they stand always gets c. Yet a time delay can be measured for light sent from Earth past the Sun to Venus and back.

paragraphs.heading: Clocks put to the test
paragraphs.text: The first direct confirmation came from the Pound–Rebka experiment in 1959, later refined by Gravity Probe A. In the Hafele–Keating experiment, atomic clocks flown on airplanes ran slightly faster than clocks on the ground. Laboratory clocks have shown the effect over height differences of less than one metre, and it has turned up in the light of the white dwarf Sirius B and in signals to and from the Viking 1 lander on Mars. The effect is large enough that the atomic clocks on GPS satellites had to be permanently corrected.

paragraphs.heading: Gravity and speed
paragraphs.text: One result ties the effect to speed. Under certain conditions on spacetime, the time dilation at the bottom of a gravity well equals the time dilation from moving at the speed needed to escape that well. For a body that falls in from very far away, the slowing caused by the speed it picks up matches the slowing caused by the well itself. To see much larger effects than on Earth, one would need to measure farther from Earth or near a bigger source of gravity.
